analysis.one_liner: Raises Social Security benefits and pays for it by lifting the payroll tax cap and taxing high earners' investment income.
analysis.headline: Introduced July 21, 2026 with 4 Democratic cosponsors and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has had no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would increase Social Security checks across the board, make the annual inflation adjustment use the index that reflects what seniors actually buy, raise the minimum benefit for people who worked decades at low wages, add credits for years spent caring for children or ailing relatives, end the five-month wait for disability benefits, and let children of deceased or disabled workers keep benefits while in college until age 26. To pay for it, it would remove the cap on wages subject to the Social Security payroll tax and apply that same 12.4% tax to investment income above $400,000. It would also rebuild Social Security's customer service staff and keep field offices open. Most of the benefit increases are written to run for 2027 through 2036 only, a ten-year window that fits Senate budget rules allowing certain bills to pass with a simple majority; the taxes, however, do not expire.
analysis.who_benefits: Retirees, disabled workers, surviving spouses, and children of deceased or disabled workers — especially low earners, long-time caregivers, and households currently taxed on their benefits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retirees, disabled workers, widows, and students

how_it_helps.text: Raises the main benefit formula from 90% to 93% of a worker's average indexed earnings, an across-the-board increase for new and existing beneficiaries.
Switches the annual cost-of-living adjustment to whichever index is higher — the standard wage-earner index or the index tracking spending typical of people 62 and older.
Creates a new minimum benefit tied to the federal poverty line, reaching 125% of poverty after 30 or more years of work, for people with long careers at low wages.
Raises the income thresholds at which Social Security benefits become taxable to $35,000 for single filers and $50,000 for joint filers, cutting taxes for moderate-income retirees.
Improves benefits for widows and widowers in two-earner households, and adds a gradual benefit increase for anyone who has been on the rolls 15 years or more.
Lets years spent caring for a child under 12 or a chronically dependent relative count as covered earnings, up to five years.

Ends the five-month waiting period before disability benefits begin and replaces the rule that cuts off disability benefits entirely once earnings rise, with a $1-reduction-for-every-$2-earned phase-out so people can try working without losing everything.
Extends children's benefits for students in at least half-time college attendance up to age 26, and makes it easier for children living with grandparents or other relatives to qualify.

Restores the system's finances by applying the 12.4% Social Security payroll tax to all wages (currently wages above roughly $180,000 are exempt) and to net investment income above $400,000, while counting that high earnings in the benefit formula at a small 1% rate.
Directs rebuilding of the agency's customer service workforce and keeping field offices open, after years of understaffing and office closures.

analysis.who_pays: High-income households: everyone earning above the wage cap pays Social Security tax on every dollar of wages, and people with investment income above $400,000 pay an added 12.4% on it. Self-employed workers above the cap also pay the full combined rate.

drawbacks.text: The added tax is steep at the top: removing the wage cap means the full 12.4% combined payroll tax applies to every dollar of wages, and investment income above $400,000 bears the same 12.4% on top of the existing 3.8% Medicare tax — a real cost for professionals, small-business owners, and wealthy retirees.

Most of the benefit improvements are written to expire after 2036; if Congress did not extend them, benefits would drop back to current-law levels, while the new taxes would remain — a structural imbalance a critic could call a tax increase with a temporary benefit promise.

Earnings above the current cap count in the benefit formula at only 1%, so the highest earners would pay far more into the system over their lifetimes relative to what they get back, which opponents describe as breaking the link between contributions and benefits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades a clear, broad benefit increase and stronger service delivery for a large, permanent tax increase concentrated on the top few percent of earners. It would also shore up the trust fund rather than drain it, which distinguishes it from pure benefit expansions. The main design weakness is the 2036 sunset on the benefit side, which creates uncertainty that supporters would need to fix in any final law.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late July 2026 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Sen. Blumenthal introduced the Social Security 2100 Act in the Senate on July 21, 2026, joined by Sens. Slotkin, Lujan, Whitehouse, and Duckworth.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance on the day it was introduced.
It has 4 cosponsors, all Democrats, and has had no further committee or floor action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nobody new: high earners have not begun paying the new taxes, and beneficiaries have not received the increases. If the bill dies quietly, the status quo benefits high-income households, who keep the current wage cap and untaxed investment income.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo so far; high earners benefit if it dies

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate Finance Committee.

for.name: Sens. Slotkin, Lujan, Whitehouse, and Duckworth

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on July 21, 2026 and has taken no action on it since — no hearing, markup, or vote.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and all 4 cosponsors are Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the Republican-held Finance Committee has not acted on it.

industries.note: The bill removes the cap so Social Security's 12.4% tax applies to every dollar of wages instead of stopping near $180,000. Higher earners would pay tens of thousands of dollars more per year, funding benefit increases for everyone else.
Investment income above $400,000 would bear an added 12.4% tax on top of the existing 3.8% Medicare contribution, the first time the retirement payroll tax reaches capital returns.

industries.industry: Self-employed professionals and small-business owners above the wage cap
industries.note: The self-employment tax cap would be lifted too, so business owners and independent professionals above the cap would pay the full combined rate on all net earnings.

analysis.trajectory: The Senate session ends January 3, 2027. A bill introduced in late July with 4 cosponsors and no committee action almost never reaches the floor on its own; the realistic paths are that it dies when the Congress ends, or that its provisions are folded into a larger tax or budget package — its 2027–2036 benefit sunsets are built to fit the Senate rules that let such packages pass with a simple majority.
